Keep it open in a browser tab while working through the markdowns. Use the language toggle above to switch between **R** and **Python**.

## Variables & Assignments

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Assigning values</h3>
```

Use `<-` or `=` to assign a value to a variable. R is **case-sensitive** — `hello` and `Hello` are different objects.

```r
a   <- 2            # numeric
b   <- TRUE         # logical
name <- "Rosalinde" # character (string)

a + 3               # use in calculations: returns 5
print(name)         # explicitly print to console
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>str(x)</td><td>Show structure and type of x</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ls()</td><td>List all objects in the environment</td></tr>
  <tr><td>rm(x)</td><td>Remove variable x from the environment</td></tr>
  <tr><td>load("file.RData")</td><td>Reload a saved environment</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

---

## Vectors

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing vectors</h3>
```

A vector is a sequence of values of the **same type**. When you mix types, R converts everything to the lowest common type (logical → numeric → character).

```r
y <- c(9, 3, 7, 2)   # numeric vector of length 4
length(y)             # 4

# Indexing
y[3]          # 7        — third element
y[2:4]        # 3 7 2    — elements 2 to 4
y[-2]         # 9 7 2    — all except element 2
y[y < 5]      # 3 2      — elements where condition is TRUE

# Logical tests (applied to each element)
y < 5         # FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE
sum(y < 5)    # 2  — count of elements satisfying condition

# Modifying
y[1] <- 10    # replace first element
```

```{=html}
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>TRUE / FALSE in arithmetic:</strong> R treats <code>TRUE</code> as 1 and <code>FALSE</code> as 0.
  So <code>sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE))</code> = 3 — a quick way to count matching elements.
</div>
</div>
```

---

## Matrices

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing matrices</h3>
```

A matrix is a **2-dimensional** structure. All elements must be the same type. Indexing uses `[row, column]` — leave one side empty to select all.

```r
X <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    2    3
# [2,]    4    5    6

dim(X)        # c(2, 3)  — rows, then columns
X[1, 2]       # 2        — row 1, column 2
X[2, ]        # 4 5 6    — entire second row
X[, 1]        # 1 4      — entire first column

# Building from vectors
A <- cbind(c(1,2), c(3,4), c(5,6))   # join as columns
B <- rbind(c(1,2,3), c(4,5,6))       # join as rows

# Naming
rownames(A) <- c("r1", "r2")
colnames(A) <- c("p1", "p2", "p3")
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>dim(X)</td><td>Returns c(rows, columns)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>nrow(X) / ncol(X)</td><td>Number of rows / columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>cbind(x, y)</td><td>Combine vectors as columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>rbind(x, y)</td><td>Combine vectors as rows</td></tr>
  <tr><td>colnames(X)</td><td>Get or set column names</td></tr>
  <tr><td>rownames(X)</td><td>Get or set row names</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Lists

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing lists</h3>
```

Lists can hold **elements of different types and lengths** — unlike vectors or matrices. Access elements with `$name` or `[[ ]]`.

```r
L <- list(color = c("blue", "red"), size = 5, active = TRUE)

# Accessing content (returns the actual value)
L$color           # "blue" "red"
L[["color"]]      # same — "blue" "red"
L[["color"]][2]   # "red"

# Single brackets return a list, not the content
L["color"]        # a list of length 1 (not the vector!)
length(L["color"])   # 1
length(L[["color"]]) # 2

# Modifying & deleting
L[["size"]] <- 10     # change an element
L[["new"]]  <- "hi"   # add a new element
L[[3]] <- NULL         # delete third element
```

```{=html}
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>[ ] vs [[ ]]:</strong> Single brackets always return a <em>list</em>.
  Double brackets return the <em>content</em>. Use <code>[[ ]]</code> when you want to work with the value.
</div>
</div>
```

---

## Dataframes

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing dataframes</h3>
```

A dataframe is like a table: rows are observations, columns are variables. Unlike matrices, **different columns can have different types**.

```r
Name   <- c("Ben", "Alice", "Daniel", "Charlie")
Year   <- c(1990, 1992, 1995, 1993)
Option <- c("Biology", "Physics", "Chemistry", "Mathematics")

df <- data.frame(First_Name = Name, Year = Year, Options = Option)

# Accessing columns
df$Year           # 1990 1992 1995 1993
df[["Year"]]      # same
df[, 2]           # same — all rows, column 2

# Accessing elements
df$Options[3]     # "Chemistry"
df[2:3, 3]        # "Physics" "Chemistry"

# Merging two dataframes
Full_Names <- data.frame(First_Name = c("Alice","Ben"),
                         Last_Name  = c("Parker","James"))

merge(df, Full_Names)          # Inner join — only matching rows
merge(df, Full_Names, all=TRUE) # Outer join — all rows, NA for missing
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>data.frame(...)</td><td>Create a dataframe from named vectors</td></tr>
  <tr><td>as.data.frame(X)</td><td>Convert a matrix to a dataframe</td></tr>
  <tr><td>dim(df)</td><td>Rows and columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>colnames(df)</td><td>Column names</td></tr>
  <tr><td>str(df)</td><td>Structure overview (types, first values)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>merge(a, b)</td><td>Join two dataframes on shared columns</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Loops & Iteration

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>apply family &amp; for loops</h3>
```

```r
Mat <- matrix(rnorm(12), nrow = 3)

apply(Mat, 1, mean)   # mean of each ROW    (MARGIN = 1)
apply(Mat, 2, mean)   # mean of each COLUMN (MARGIN = 2)

x <- c(1:5)
sapply(x, sqrt)       # apply sqrt() to each element → returns vector
lapply(x, sqrt)       # same but returns a list

# For loop
for (i in 1:4) {
  print(i * 3)
}

# If / else
a <- 5; b <- 10
if (a < b) { print("a is smaller") } else { print("b is smaller") }
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>apply(X, 1, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each row of matrix/dataframe</td></tr>
  <tr><td>apply(X, 2, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each column</td></tr>
  <tr><td>sapply(x, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each element of vector/list → vector</td></tr>
  <tr><td>lapply(x, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each element → list</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Index Selection

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>which, %in%, is.na</h3>
```

```r
x <- c(2, 8, 3, 7, 1)

which(x > 5)          # c(2, 4)  — INDICES where condition is TRUE
x[which(x > 5)]       # c(8, 7)  — VALUES at those indices

c("a","b","c") %in% c("b","d")  # FALSE TRUE FALSE
                                 # — is each element in the right-hand set?

is.na(c(1, NA, 3))    # FALSE TRUE FALSE
sum(is.na(x))         # count of NA values
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function / Operator</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>which(condition)</td><td>Returns indices where condition is TRUE</td></tr>
  <tr><td>x %in% y</td><td>For each element of x: is it anywhere in y?</td></tr>
  <tr><td>is.na(x)</td><td>TRUE for each NA element</td></tr>
  <tr><td>na.omit(x)</td><td>Remove NA values from a vector or dataframe</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## dplyr: Data Manipulation

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>The core verbs &amp; the pipe</h3>
```

`dplyr` provides a small set of **verbs** to work on dataframes. Each verb takes a dataframe as first argument and returns a new dataframe. Column names are written **without quotes and without `df$`**. Install once with `install.packages("dplyr")`, then load it in every session.

```r
library(dplyr)

head(iris)    # built-in data set: 150 flowers, 3 species

# filter(): keep ROWS that satisfy a condition
filter(iris, Species == "setosa")
filter(iris, Sepal.Length > 7, Species != "setosa")   # comma = AND

# select(): keep COLUMNS
select(iris, Sepal.Length, Species)
select(iris, -Petal.Width)           # all columns except Petal.Width

# arrange(): sort rows
arrange(iris, desc(Sepal.Length))    # largest first

# mutate(): add or change columns
mutate(iris, Sepal.Ratio = Sepal.Length / Sepal.Width)
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>filter(df, cond)</td><td>Keep the rows where the condition is TRUE</td></tr>
  <tr><td>select(df, a, b)</td><td>Keep (or with <code>-a</code> drop) columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>arrange(df, a)</td><td>Sort rows by a (use <code>desc(a)</code> for descending)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>mutate(df, new = ...)</td><td>Create a new column or modify an existing one</td></tr>
  <tr><td>rename(df, new = old)</td><td>Rename a column</td></tr>
  <tr><td>distinct(df, a)</td><td>Unique values (rows) of a</td></tr>
</table>
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>The pipe <code>|&gt;</code>:</strong> <code>x |&gt; f(y)</code> means <code>f(x, y)</code> — read it as
  "and then". It lets you chain several steps without nesting functions or creating temporary variables.
  <code>|&gt;</code> is built into R (&ge; 4.1); the older <code>%&gt;%</code> (loaded with dplyr) works the same way.
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Group, summarise &amp; join</h3>
```

`group_by()` splits the data into groups, and `summarise()` then computes **one row per group**. This replaces many `sapply()`/`apply()` loops.

```r
iris |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  summarise(n           = n(),
            mean_length = mean(Sepal.Length),
            sd_length   = sd(Sepal.Length))

count(iris, Species)      # shortcut: number of rows per group

# A typical chain: filter -> new column -> summary
iris |>
  filter(Sepal.Length > 5) |>
  mutate(Sepal.Ratio = Sepal.Length / Sepal.Width) |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  summarise(mean_ratio = mean(Sepal.Ratio))

# Joining two dataframes (df and Full_Names from the Dataframes section)
left_join(df, Full_Names, by = "First_Name")   # keep all rows of df
inner_join(df, Full_Names, by = "First_Name")  # keep only matching rows
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>group_by(df, a)</td><td>Split the data into groups defined by a</td></tr>
  <tr><td>summarise(df, m = mean(x))</td><td>Collapse each group to one row of summary values</td></tr>
  <tr><td>n()</td><td>Number of rows in the current group (inside summarise/mutate)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>count(df, a)</td><td>Number of rows per value of a</td></tr>
  <tr><td>left_join(a, b, by = "id")</td><td>Add the columns of b to a, matching on id</td></tr>
  <tr><td>inner_join(a, b, by = "id")</td><td>Keep only rows present in both</td></tr>
</table>
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>Tip:</strong> the result of <code>summarise()</code> is again a dataframe, so you can pass it straight
  into <code>ggplot()</code> (next section) or save it with <code>result &lt;- ...</code>.
</div>
</div>
```

## ggplot2: Plotting

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Building a plot in layers</h3>
```

A `ggplot2` plot is built **layer by layer**, joined with `+`: first the data and the **aesthetic mapping** `aes()` (which column goes on which axis / colour), then one or more **geoms** that draw the data, then optional labels, scales and themes.

```r
library(ggplot2)

# Scatter plot, coloured by species
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Sepal length (cm)", y = "Sepal width (cm)", title = "Iris sepals")

# Other common plot types
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20)
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.5)

# One panel per species
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Species)

# Reference line + own colours
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(iris$Sepal.Length), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(setosa = "#C61826", versicolor = "#590D08", virginica = "#4A4743")) +
  theme_minimal()

# dplyr + ggplot2: summarise first, then plot
iris |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  summarise(mean_length = mean(Sepal.Length)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Species, y = mean_length)) +
  geom_col()

ggsave("plot.png", width = 6, height = 4)   # saves the last plot
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>ggplot(data, aes(x, y))</td><td>Start a plot: data and aesthetic mapping</td></tr>
  <tr><td>geom_point() / geom_line()</td><td>Points / lines</td></tr>
  <tr><td>geom_histogram() / geom_density()</td><td>Distribution of one variable</td></tr>
  <tr><td>geom_boxplot()</td><td>Boxplot per group</td></tr>
  <tr><td>geom_col() / geom_bar()</td><td>Bars from a value column / from counts</td></tr>
  <tr><td>geom_vline() / geom_hline()</td><td>Vertical / horizontal reference line</td></tr>
  <tr><td>facet_wrap(~ a)</td><td>One panel per value of a</td></tr>
  <tr><td>labs(x, y, title)</td><td>Axis labels and title</td></tr>
  <tr><td>scale_color_manual(values = ...)</td><td>Choose your own colours</td></tr>
  <tr><td>theme_minimal()</td><td>Clean look (also theme_bw(), theme_classic())</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ggsave("file.png")</td><td>Save the last plot to a file</td></tr>
</table>
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>Two common mistakes:</strong> (1) the <code>+</code> must be at the <em>end</em> of a line, not at the
  start of the next one. (2) Variables from your data go <em>inside</em> <code>aes()</code>
  (<code>aes(color = Species)</code>); a fixed value goes <em>outside</em> (<code>geom_point(color = "red")</code>).
  Also remember that <code>ggplot()</code> needs a <strong>dataframe</strong>, not a bare vector.
</div>
</div>

</div><!-- end .lang-r -->
<div class="lang-python">
```

## Variables & Assignments

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>Assigning values</h3>
```

Use `=` to assign a value to a variable. Python is **case-sensitive** — `hello` and `Hello` are different objects. There is no `<-` operator in Python.

```python
a    = 2              # integer
b    = True           # boolean  (note capital T)
name = "Rosalinde"   # string

a + 3                # 5
print(name)          # Rosalinde
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>type(x)</td><td>Show the type of x</td></tr>
  <tr><td>dir()</td><td>List all names in the current scope</td></tr>
  <tr><td>del x</td><td>Remove variable x</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Lists

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing lists (R: vectors)</h3>
```

Python lists use **0-based indexing** and can hold mixed types. Use `[ ]` for indexing and slicing.

```python
y = [9, 3, 7, 2]    # list of length 4
len(y)               # 4

# Indexing (0-based!)
y[2]                 # 7        — third element (index 2)
y[1:3]               # [3, 7]   — elements at index 1 and 2
y[:-1]               # [9,3,7]  — all except last

# Filter with list comprehension
[x for x in y if x < 5]      # [3, 2]
[x < 5 for x in y]           # [False, True, False, True]
sum(x < 5 for x in y)        # 2  — count matching

# Modifying
y[0] = 10            # replace first element (index 0)
```

```{=html}
<div class="tip-box" style="background:#ECE8E1;border-left-color:#4A4743;">
  <strong>Mixed types:</strong> Unlike R vectors, Python lists allow mixed types:
  <code>[True, "hello", 3]</code> stays as-is — no automatic conversion.
  Indexing starts at <strong>0</strong>, not 1.
</div>
</div>
```

---

## NumPy Arrays

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing arrays (R: matrices)</h3>
```

NumPy arrays are the Python equivalent of R matrices. Requires `import numpy as np`. Indexing is **0-based**.

```python
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])
# Shape: (2, 3)

X.shape          # (2, 3)  — rows, then columns
X[0, 1]          # 2       — row 0, column 1 (0-based!)
X[1, :]          # [4 5 6] — entire second row
X[:, 0]          # [1 4]   — entire first column

# Building from vectors
A = np.column_stack(([1,2], [3,4], [5,6]))  # join as columns
B = np.vstack([[1,2,3], [4,5,6]])            # join as rows
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>X.shape</td><td>Returns (rows, columns) as a tuple</td></tr>
  <tr><td>X.reshape(r, c)</td><td>Reshape to r rows and c columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>np.hstack((a, b))</td><td>Combine arrays side by side (columns)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>np.vstack((a, b))</td><td>Stack arrays vertically (rows)</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Dictionaries

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing dicts (R: lists)</h3>
```

Dictionaries hold **key–value pairs** of any type. Use `[ ]` with the key to access values — there is no `$` or `[[ ]]` in Python.

```python
L = {"color": ["blue", "red"], "size": 5, "active": True}

# Accessing content
L["color"]           # ["blue", "red"]
L["color"][1]        # "red"   — second element (0-based)

# Check if key exists
"color" in L         # True

# Modifying & deleting
L["size"] = 10       # change a value
L["new"]  = "hi"     # add a new key
del L["size"]        # delete a key
```

```{=html}
<div class="tip-box" style="background:#ECE8E1;border-left-color:#4A4743;">
  <strong>R vs Python:</strong> R's <code>L[["color"]]</code> → Python's <code>L["color"]</code>.
  Square brackets always return the value directly in Python — no double-bracket distinction.
</div>
</div>
```

## DataFrames

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing DataFrames (R: data.frame)</h3>
```

Pandas DataFrames are the Python equivalent of R dataframes. Requires `import pandas as pd`.

```python
import pandas as pd

Name   = ["Ben", "Alice", "Daniel", "Charlie"]
Year   = [1990, 1992, 1995, 1993]
Option = ["Biology", "Physics", "Chemistry", "Mathematics"]

df = pd.DataFrame({"First_Name": Name, "Year": Year, "Options": Option})

# Accessing columns
df["Year"]            # Series: 1990 1992 1995 1993
df.Year               # same — attribute-style access
df.iloc[:, 1]         # same — all rows, column index 1 (0-based)

# Accessing elements
df["Options"].iloc[2]    # "Chemistry"
df.iloc[1:3, 2]          # "Physics", "Chemistry"

# Merging two DataFrames
Full_Names = pd.DataFrame({"First_Name": ["Alice","Ben"],
                            "Last_Name":  ["Parker","James"]})

pd.merge(df, Full_Names)                    # Inner join — matching rows only
pd.merge(df, Full_Names, how="outer")       # Outer join — all rows, NaN for missing
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>pd.DataFrame({...})</td><td>Create a DataFrame from a dict of lists</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.shape</td><td>Rows and columns as (r, c)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.columns</td><td>Column names</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.dtypes</td><td>Data type of each column</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.describe()</td><td>Summary statistics for numeric columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>pd.merge(a, b)</td><td>Join two DataFrames on shared columns</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Loops & Iteration

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>for loops, list comprehensions &amp; numpy</h3>
```

```python
import numpy as np

Mat = np.random.randn(3, 4)

np.mean(Mat, axis=0)        # mean of each COLUMN
np.mean(Mat, axis=1)        # mean of each ROW

x = list(range(1, 6))       # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
[np.sqrt(i) for i in x]     # list comprehension — apply to each element
list(map(np.sqrt, x))        # same result with map()

# For loop
for i in range(1, 5):
    print(i * 3)

# If / else
a = 5; b = 10
if a < b:
    print("a is smaller")
else:
    print("b is smaller")
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function / Syntax</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>np.mean(X, axis=0)</td><td>Mean of each column (axis 0 = rows collapse)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>np.mean(X, axis=1)</td><td>Mean of each row (axis 1 = columns collapse)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>[f(x) for x in lst]</td><td>List comprehension — apply f to each element</td></tr>
  <tr><td>map(f, lst)</td><td>Apply f to each element → map object</td></tr>
  <tr><td>filter(f, lst)</td><td>Keep elements where f returns True</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Index Selection

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>np.where, in, pd.isna</h3>
```

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

x = np.array([2, 8, 3, 7, 1])

np.where(x > 5)          # (array([1, 3]),)  — INDICES where condition is TRUE
x[np.where(x > 5)]       # array([8, 7])     — VALUES at those indices
x[x > 5]                 # array([8, 7])     — direct boolean indexing (shortcut)

"a" in ["b", "d"]        # False  — membership test
["a" in ["b","d"], "b" in ["b","d"], "c" in ["b","d"]]  # [False, True, False]

pd.isna(pd.Series([1, None, 3]))   # [False, True, False]
np.isnan(x.astype(float))          # array of bool (for float arrays)
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function / Operator</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>np.where(condition)</td><td>Returns tuple of indices where condition is TRUE</td></tr>
  <tr><td>x in y</td><td>True if x appears in sequence y</td></tr>
  <tr><td>pd.isna(x)</td><td>True for each NaN / None element</td></tr>
  <tr><td>np.isnan(x)</td><td>True for each NaN in a NumPy float array</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.dropna()</td><td>Remove rows with any missing value</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## pandas: Data Manipulation (R: dplyr)

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>Filter, select, sort, new columns, group &amp; summarise</h3>
```

`pandas` does everything R's `dplyr` does. Here the column names are **strings** and you work with the DataFrame methods (`df.method()`). The example uses the iris data set that ships with seaborn.

```python
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

iris = sns.load_dataset("iris")   # columns: sepal_length, sepal_width, petal_length, petal_width, species
iris.head()

# filter: keep ROWS that satisfy a condition   (R: filter)
iris[iris["species"] == "setosa"]
iris.query("sepal_length > 7 and species != 'setosa'")    # same idea, readable text condition

# select: keep COLUMNS                         (R: select)
iris[["sepal_length", "species"]]
iris.drop(columns="petal_width")                          # all columns except petal_width

# sort                                          (R: arrange)
iris.sort_values("sepal_length", ascending=False)

# new column                                    (R: mutate)
iris.assign(sepal_ratio = iris["sepal_length"] / iris["sepal_width"])

# group + summarise                             (R: group_by + summarise)
iris.groupby("species").agg(n           = ("species", "size"),
                            mean_length = ("sepal_length", "mean"),
                            sd_length   = ("sepal_length", "std"))

iris["species"].value_counts()                            # (R: count)

# Chain several steps with parentheses            (R: the |> pipe)
(iris
   .query("sepal_length > 5")
   .groupby("species")
   .agg(mean_length=("sepal_length", "mean"))
   .reset_index())
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does (R equivalent)</th></tr>
  <tr><td>df[df["a"] &gt; 5]  /  df.query("a &gt; 5")</td><td>Keep rows matching a condition (filter)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df[["a", "b"]]  /  df.drop(columns="a")</td><td>Keep / drop columns (select)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.sort_values("a")</td><td>Sort rows (arrange)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.assign(new = ...)</td><td>Add or change a column (mutate)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.rename(columns={"old": "new"})</td><td>Rename a column (rename)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df.groupby("a").agg(m=("x", "mean"))</td><td>Group and summarise (group_by + summarise)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>df["a"].value_counts()</td><td>Number of rows per value (count)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>pd.merge(a, b, on="id", how="left")</td><td>Join two DataFrames (left_join)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>.reset_index()</td><td>Turn the group labels back into a normal column</td></tr>
</table>
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>Tip:</strong> most pandas methods <em>return a new DataFrame</em> and leave the original unchanged.
  Save the result (<code>result = iris.query(...)</code>) if you want to keep it.
  After <code>groupby().agg()</code> the group names sit in the index — <code>.reset_index()</code> moves them back into a column.
</div>
</div>
```

## Plotting: matplotlib &amp; seaborn (R: ggplot2)

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section py">
<h3>Quick plots with seaborn, fine-tuning with matplotlib</h3>
```

`seaborn` draws statistical plots directly from a DataFrame (like `ggplot2`); `matplotlib` (`plt`) is the layer underneath, used for labels, titles, reference lines and saving. In seaborn you pass `data=` and the **column names** for `x`, `y` and `hue` (= colour groups, like `color`/`fill` in `aes()`).

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Scatter plot, coloured by species
sns.scatterplot(data=iris, x="sepal_length", y="sepal_width", hue="species")
plt.xlabel("Sepal length (cm)")
plt.ylabel("Sepal width (cm)")
plt.title("Iris sepals")
plt.show()

# Other common plot types
sns.histplot(data=iris, x="sepal_length", bins=20)
sns.boxplot(data=iris, x="species", y="sepal_length")
sns.kdeplot(data=iris, x="sepal_length", hue="species", fill=True, alpha=0.5)

# One panel per species                          (R: facet_wrap)
sns.relplot(data=iris, x="sepal_length", y="sepal_width", col="species")

# Reference line + own colours
sns.scatterplot(data=iris, x="sepal_length", y="sepal_width", hue="species",
                palette={"setosa": "#C61826", "versicolor": "#590D08", "virginica": "#4A4743"})
plt.axvline(iris["sepal_length"].mean(), linestyle="--")

# dplyr-style summary first, then plot
means = iris.groupby("species").agg(mean_length=("sepal_length", "mean")).reset_index()
sns.barplot(data=means, x="species", y="mean_length")

plt.savefig("plot.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")   # call BEFORE plt.show()
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does (R equivalent)</th></tr>
  <tr><td>sns.scatterplot(data, x, y, hue)</td><td>Scatter plot (geom_point)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>sns.lineplot(...)</td><td>Line plot (geom_line)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>sns.histplot() / sns.kdeplot()</td><td>Histogram / density (geom_histogram, geom_density)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>sns.boxplot()</td><td>Boxplot per group (geom_boxplot)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>sns.barplot()</td><td>Bars of a mean (or other estimate) per group (geom_col)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>sns.relplot(..., col="a")</td><td>One panel per value of a (facet_wrap)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>plt.axvline() / plt.axhline()</td><td>Vertical / horizontal reference line (geom_vline / geom_hline)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>plt.xlabel() / plt.ylabel() / plt.title()</td><td>Axis labels and title (labs)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>plt.savefig("file.png")</td><td>Save the figure (ggsave)</td></tr>
</table>
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>Tip:</strong> if you prefer the <code>ggplot2</code> syntax (<code>ggplot(...) + geom_point()</code>) in Python,
  the optional package <code>plotnine</code> offers it. In this course we use <code>matplotlib</code>
  and <code>seaborn</code>, as in the Python notebooks.
</div>
</div>

</div><!-- end .lang-python -->
```
